9. DIRECTORATES 
9.] Centre for Audit Quality Directorate (CAQD) 


The ICAI established the Centre for Audit Quality Directorate (““CAQD”) in 2020, primarily focusing on the 
qualitative aspects of the audit function and audit quality. It is a Special Purpose Directorate, ensuring consistent 
improvement in audit quality and boost in Indian firm’s global standing. It also seeks to provide a conducive 
environment for research and to take up more research-oriented projects to set the criteria for enhancing and 
maintaining the Audit Quality. It supports research programs on Audit Quality by enhancing interactions among 
various stakeholders and regulators involved in law enforcement. The Centre for Audit Quality Directorate is 
aiming at continuous investment in the contemporary education and training for professional accountants and 
auditors through Special short term duration courses for participants to induct the requisite skill set on the 
contemporary areas. It strives to develop guidance and training programmes to assist audit teams to undertake 
effective root cause analysis for audit quality improvement. 


ACTIVITIES UNDERTAKEN BY CENTRE FOR AUDIT QUALITY DIRECTORATE 
(I) UTILITIES DEVELOPED BY CAQ 


The CAQD develops and provides technological resources to members to facilitate smooth conduct of quality audit 
and assurance. In line with this objective, the CAQD continued its efforts to support audit firms by developing and 
updating various tools and utilities aimed at enhancing audit quality, operational efficiency, and regulatory 
compliance. 


During the year, the following utilities were developed/ updated: 


e Utility for self-evaluation under AQMM v 2.0- Release of a new Utility- This Utility will assist the firms 
to self -evaluate their firm’s maturity level on the basis of Audit Quality Indicators defined under AQMM v 
2.0. This will enable the firms to identify areas where competencies are strong or lacking and then develop a 
road map for achieving a higher level of audit maturity. 


e Utility for Bank Branch Audit- 2025 Edition- Updation of existing Utility- To help the members in 
smooth conduct of the bank branch audits, the Centre for Audit Quality Directorate (CAQD) has developed 
an excel utility based on the Guidance Note on Audit of Banks and the Technical Guide on Long Form 
Audit Report issued by AASB. The Utility for Bank Branch Audit- 2025 Edition has been updated, 
incorporating the changes in the Guidance Note on Audit of Banks (2025 Edition). 


In the previous years, the Directorate had successfully introduced several key utilities, including: 


e Utility for Determining Materiality: The Utility assists auditors in assessing audit materiality thresholds 
by categorizing risk parameters and evaluating the impact of material misstatements. 


e Reviewing and Monitoring Tool on Standards on Auditing Compliance: The Tool facilitates 
compliance with Standards on Auditing by providing comprehensive checklists, enabling easy review, 
monitoring, and documentation. Progress is tracked through a ‘Work Status’ feature summarized in the 
Dashboard. 


[भाग [--खण्ड 4] भारत का राजपत्र : असाधारण 28] 


e Utility on Engagement Letters: The Utility streamlines the generation of engagement letters for assurance 
clients, enabling auditors to efficiently create multiple letters using a customizable template, saving time and 
reducing complexity.

significantly to India’s global trade aspiration.

9.9 Legal Directorate 


(0) The Supreme Court in Shaji Paulose vs. ICAI upholds ICAI Guidelines on number of Tax audits 
under Section 44AB of the Income Tax Act, 96]. 


290 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY [PART III—SEC.4] 


The Supreme Court vide its judgment dated 7.05.2024 upheld the Guidelines dated 08.08.2008 issued by ICAI 
that had set a ceiling on the number of tax audit assignments which can be undertaken by a Chartered Accountant. 
The Court has ruled that the ICAI Guidelines are not violative of the fundamental right to practice profession 
guaranteed under Article l(g) of the Constitution of India and the same are in public interest and therefore saved by 
Article 9(2) of the Constitution of India. Since the 989 Notification was struck down by the Madras High Court 
and in view of the conflicting judgments of different High Courts, the ICAI has approached the Supreme Court and 
filed a Transfer Petition seeking transfer of writ petitions pending in various High Courts to the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court itself for final determination of the issue. Applying the doctrine of legal uncertainty, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court was pleased to quash the disciplinary proceedings initiated against the petitioners as well as similarly situated 
members. 


Liberty is given to the Institute to revise the maximum number of tax audits under Section 44AB. Liberty was also 
granted to the petitioners to make a representation to the Institute to this effect and the Institute may consider the 
same. In addition to the aforesaid directions, the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the course of the judgment has paid 
rich compliments and appreciated the ICAI for playing a significant role in ensuring the dynamism of the CA 
Course and the role and responsibility of Chartered Accountants in the economic development. The Supreme Court 
has further observed as under: - 


"ICAI has, over time, received recognition as a premier accounting body domestically and globally for maintaining 
the highest standards...the ICAI has also played a significant role in ensuring the dynamism of the CA course and 
the credibility of the examination. We commend that the ICAI must be committed towards the convergence of 
accounting and ethical standards with international standards.” 


The Supreme Court further observed that quality, reliability and objectivity of the information certified by 
Chartered Accountants are relied upon by stakeholders to make commercial decisions and allocate resources. 
Transparent accounting is necessary to strengthen credibility of the financial markets, market participants, investors 
and other stakeholders. It is, therefore, not surprising to find that the accounting profession is being constantly 
challenged to meet the ever-increasing demands for quality information or for verification of the financial 
statements. The higher the quality and integrity maintained by the profession, the stronger and more resilient will 
our financial markets be. The accounting profession facilities market discipline and renders confidence amongst 
various stakeholders and reduce the possibility of irregularities in the financial markets. More importantly, 
Chartered Accountants themselves have to comply with the relevant laws and regulations. The Chartered 
Accountants must refuse to represent clients who insist on resorting to unfair means. Chartered Accountants are 
relevant not only to securing corporate governance but governance in broader context too. Chartered Accountants 
assume different responsibilities towards tax administration, to the client and to the economy at large. In that 
context, we stress on the importance of preserving their independence of views and integrity to separate their client 
advisory role from their role as public citizens seeking to improve the functioning of the tax administration of the 
nation. Integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care and confidentiality must be the doctrines 
guiding the work ethic. 


(II) Batch of Writ petitions filed in MAF matters challenging the disciplinary proceedings conducted by 
ICAI 


Batch of writ petitions were filed by the partners of MAF seeking to be released from disciplinary proceedings 
being conducted by ICAI as they are not nominated ‘members concerned’ in the proceedings for misconduct as per 
Rule 8 of the Chartered Accountants (Procedure of Investigation of Professional & Other Misconduct and Conduct 
of Cases) Rules, 2007. 


The Hon’ble Court vide its judgment dated 22™ March 2024 (pronounced on 03" July, 2024) held as under at para 
99 of the judgement: - 


“Thus, in a case, where there is any complaint or allegation in respect of a single incident or an act of a member, 
the firm can designate that particular person, who was associated with the said act, which is alleged to be 
misconduct. The position would however not be the same, in a case where the allegations are in respect of 
arrangements entered into by firms with other international counterparts, spanning over decades and multiple 
agreements. A single individual cannot be pinned down in such situations to be responsible for answering the 
complaint as ‘member answerable’. The firm as a whole has to be held responsible if found culpable, in such 


, 


circumstances, failing which the Act would be rendered toothless.’ 


[भाग ता--खण्ड 4] भारत का राजपत्र : असाधारण 29] 


The Court further held that that the writ petitions are not maintainable. It is open for the petitioners to participate in 
the disciplinary proceedings, if they so choose and file their reply on merits to the notice issued by the Disciplinary 
Committee of ICAI. 


Division Bench of High Court vide order dated .08.2024 has granted stay of the disciplinary proceedings 
initiated against the Appellants. 


(IID) W.P.(C) No.42096/209, Federation of Chartered Accountants Association (FCAA) Vs. Union of India 
& Ors. decided by Delhi High Court 


Federation of Chartered Accountants Association of India (petitioner) filed the captioned writ petition against 
Union of India through MCA, NFRA and ICAI, challenging the constitutional validity of Sections 32(2) & 32(4) 
of the Companies Act 203, which, inter alia, empower the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) to 
investigate into matters of professional or other misconduct by Chartered Accountants and impose penalties 
thereon. 


Subsequently, batch of writ petitions were filed by individual chartered accountants who were aggrieved by the 
punishment orders of NFRA. These petitions were also challenging the constitutional validity of Section 32 as 
well as the procedure adopted by NFRA in imposing the penalties. All the writ petitions were tagged and heard 
together by the Division Bench of the High Court of Delhi as they dealt with common question of law. Judgement 
was pronounced on 07th February, 2025 upholding the constitutional validity of Section 32(2) & (4) of the 
Companies Act, 20l3. However, the punishment imposed on individual Chartered Accountant were set aside on the 
ground of non-separation of investigative and quasi- judicial functions of National Financial Regulatory Authority 
(NFRA). 


NFRA has challenged the aforesaid judgment of the Division Bench of the High Court in so far as it relates to 
quashing of the Show Cause notices and punishment awarded to the individual Chartered Accountants in the 
Supreme Court. The Hon’ble Supreme Court has refused to stay the judgment of the Division Bench of High Court. 
It was also clarified by the Supreme Court that in the pending cases before the NFRA have to be dealt with in lines 
of the judgment of the High Court. 


(IV) The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India on 29% April 2025 in the case of Himanshu Singh Vs. UOI 
(popularly known as Supertech Case) had issued various directions to Government of India, 
Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, RERA, RBI, CBI and ICAI. 


Background: 


More than 70 petitions were filed by over |200 home buyers in the Supreme Court alleging systematic 
failure of statutory and government authorities to discharge their statutory functions, circumvention of 
regulatory framework by Banks and Housing Financial Corporations and the resultant illicit benefits said to 
have been drawn by builders/developers and the cost of the home by us who are now bearing the brunt of 
such failures. 


Directions to ICAI: 
In so far as ICAI is concerned, the following directions were issued: 


"|9, The President, Institute of Chartered Accountants of India is directed to deploy three Chartered 
Accountants, who are well conversant with the process of forensic audit and place them at the disposal of CBI 
to assist the Bureau/SIT in the matter of subject enquiry/investigations. The details of the remuneration to the 
paid to these Chartered Accounts be forwarded to this Court so that an appropriate order in that regard can be 
passed on the next date of hearing."

9,]4 Tender Monitoring Directorate (TMD) 


In order to monitor, analyze and streamline tendering for professional services of Chartered Accountants, a 
Directorate namely "Tender Monitoring Directorate" was constituted by the Council during the year 2023-24. The 
Directorate has been endeavouring to streamline the process of tendering and to monitor the bids quoted by CAs in 
all the permissible tenders and analyse them. The Directorate further refers the deviations at appropriate level. 


Major activities of the Directorate 


The Directorate has its own Portal for tenders on professional services — www.tmdicai.org. which offers the 
following features: 


e Tender opportunities 

e Latest information for members 

e Council Guidelines on tenders 

e Details of minimum recommended scale of fees 


e Format of cost sheet to be submitted by members

e Extract from relevant provisions of Code of Ethics 

e Representations made by Directorate to the tenderers 

e Answers to Frequently Asked Questions 

e Grievance posting mechanism, with or without disclosing identity. 

e Fee calculator for the ease of calculating fee for audit and other assignments. 


Representations are being made to tenderers where minimum fees is not prescribed in respect of audit & attestation 
services, or where eligibility conditions appear to be unreasonably restrictive or where the services tendered create 
“independence” issues. During the functional year 2024-25, [74 such representations were sent to the tendering 
organisations. During the functional year 2025-26 upto 30" May 2025, so far 5 representations have been sent. 
TMD also collects tenders for professional services from all over India and hosts the same in its TMD Portal.

TMD portal as these were found appropriate in all respects. During the current functional year upto 30™ May 
2025, so far 67 tenders have been studied, out of which 564 tenders have been hosted in the TMD portal.

amount. During the functional year 2024-25, notices were sent to 3!l CA firms in respect of 56 tenders. During 
the current functional year 2025-26, so far notices have been sent to 73 CA firms in respect of |3 tenders. During

has been ordered in respect of 56 CA firms. Cases relating to |29 CA firms have been closed as the cost sheet was 
found to be satisfactory. Examination of rest of the cases is on. During the last functional year and the current one,

9.5 UDIN Directorate 


In today’s evolving business and regulatory environment, the Unique Document Identification Number (UDIN), 
introduced by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), holds critical importance. It acts as a 
safeguard against the circulation of fraudulent financial documents by assigning a unique identifier to every 
certificate, audit report, and attestation issued by practicing chartered accountants. This mandatory requirement 
enables online verification of documents, thereby ensuring their authenticity and legitimacy. UDIN significantly 
enhances trust and transparency in financial reporting. It enables stakeholders—such as investors, regulators, and 
government bodies—to swiftly validate certified documents, thereby mitigating risks associated with 
misinformation or forgery. By enforcing accountability, UDIN promotes adherence to ethical practices and 
auditing standards, reinforcing a culture of professionalism and responsibility among chartered accountants. 


[भाग ता--खण्ड 4] भारत का राजपत्र : असाधारण 297 


The system has witnessed widespread adoption and has become an integral part of professional practices. It also 
streamlines regulatory processes by offering a standardized, technology-driven mechanism for document 
verification. This digital approach not only improves efficiency in audits and compliance checks but also aligns 
with the broader movement toward digital governance and transparency. As businesses navigate increasingly 
complex compliance landscapes, UDIN stands out as a vital tool for upholding the integrity of financial reporting. 
It fosters stakeholder confidence, supports good governance, and contributes to a more robust and transparent 
economic ecosystem. In essence, UDIN is a transformative initiative that underscores ICAI’s commitment to 
strengthening the credibility of financial reporting in India. By leveraging technology to deter fraud and ensure 
document authenticity, UDIN plays a pivotal role in promoting sustainable business growth and regulatory 
confidence. 


()  UDIN -A decision making parameter for the Regulators, Banks and Other Stakeholders 


e On 30th May 2025, ICAI showcased the UDIN system before a visiting delegation from Her Majesty’s 
Revenue and Customs (HMRC), UK, at the Centre for Taxation and Finance, New Delhi. This knowledge- 
sharing engagement, held under the collaborative “Risking of Agents” project with the Central Board of 
Direct Taxes (CBDT), reflected growing global interest in UDIN as a best practice tool. 


e In recognition of its effectiveness, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) 
acknowledged UDIN as a best practice and proposed its integration with the upcoming “Entity-Locker” 
platform a secure digital repository for storing and sharing documents of large entities, MSMEs, trusts, and 
societies. This initiative aims to streamline document management and interactions with banks, regulators, 
and other authorities. MeitY appreciated the role of UDIN in promoting trust and efficiency in digital 
governance. To enable real-time verification of CA-certified documents, MeitY approached the UDIN 
Directorate for API integration. Two meetings were held on 30th October 2024 and |7 March 2025 to 
discuss specific requirements and explore seamless API-based integration within the Entity-Locker 
framework, strengthening the credibility and traceability of documents in digital ecosystems. 


e The Director General of Supply and Transport, Indian Army, Ministry of Defence (MoD) approached the 
UDIN Directorate to provide API integration for the verification of UDIN on a real-time basis. A meeting 
was held on 23rd December 2024, to understand their specific requirements and to discuss the possibility of 
incorporating an API for real-time verification of UDINs. 


e The Chhattisgarh Real Estate Regulatory Authority (CG-RERA) approached the UDIN Directorate to 
provide an API for enabling real-time verification of UDINs through their system. Following several 
meetings with CG-RERA and subsequent approval from the competent authority, a Memorandum of 
Understanding (MoU) was signed between ICAI and CG-RERA on 5 October, 2024. This collaboration 
aims to strengthen transparency and streamline document authentication processes. 


e Orisha Real Estate Regulatory Authority (ORERA) operates on a digital platform aimed at minimizing 
physical interactions and is currently upgrading to a new system, ORERA 2.0. Certificates and approvals 
issued by Chartered Accountants often require independent verification. To facilitate this, Odisha-RERA 
sought collaboration with the UDIN Directorate to integrate their updated system (ORERA 2.0) with the 
UDIN portal for real-time UDIN verification through API. A meeting with the Odisha Real Estate 
Regulatory Authority (ORERA) was held on |8th September 2024 to understand their specific requirements 
and explore the integration of an API for seamless and real-time verification of UDINs. 


e The Comptroller and Auditor General of India (C&AG) used the UDINs as one of the elements for the 
purpose of empanelment of CA firms/LLPs by them for the first time in year 2023-24. C&AG provided the 
following scoring mechanism for empanelment of CA Firms/LLPs based on UDIN data. “For the year 2025 - 
2026, points will be awarded on the basis of UDINs generated on ICAI portal during the years 2020-202, 
202-2022, 2022-2023 and 2023-2024. This will eventually be scaled to 5 years by 2026-2027 by gradually 
adding one year on annual basis”. 


(D  UDIN Logo - official visual identity for the Unique Document Identification Number (UDIN) 
UDIN Logo Overview: 


The UDIN initiative has been widely accepted in India for enhancing transparency and professionalism in 
accounting. To reinforce its identity, ICAI launched a distinctive UDIN logo on February 0, 2025, symbolizing 
authenticity, integrity, and trust. The design features "CA" within "ICAI," representing Chartered Accountants as 
pillars of financial prudence, and a tricolor thumbprint reflecting Indian roots and the unique trust behind each 
UDIN-certified document. The logo provides a clear identity to certified documents, serves as a seal of 
authentication, and symbolizes the permanent, trustworthy nature of UDIN, strengthening credibility in financial 
reporting. 


298 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY [PART III—SEC.4] 


(It) Expression of Interest for Adoption of UDIN: The Unique Document Identification Number (UDIN) 
continues to gain international recognition, with professional bodies from other countries expressing interest 
in its adoption. 


e A meeting with the delegation from the Institute of Certified Public Accountants of Kenya (ICPAK) was 
held on 3rd February 2025 to discuss the process, framework, and protocols for implementing UDIN in 
Kenya. 


e Similarly, the National Board of Accountants and Auditors (NBAA), Tanzania expressed keen interest in 
adopting the UDIN framework. Delegations from NBAA held meetings with the UDIN Directorate in 
February and April 2023 to explore the implementation strategy. It is a matter of pride that NBAA 
acknowledged the ICAI’s initiative and conveyed their appreciation through an official letter. 


(III) Initiatives for the Members 


e On |\th October 2024, the “Gujarat Public Trust Act, 20ll” was added to the dropdown menu of statutes 
under the “Under Act / Law / Statute / Regulation” section in the “Audit and Assurance Functions” category 
on the UDIN Portal. This enabled practicing Chartered Accountants to select the statute while generating 
UDINs for relevant certifications and audit functions. Subsequently, the statute was renamed as the “Gujarat 
Public Trusts Act, |950” with effect from 8th May 2025, and the dropdown on the portal was duly updated 
to reflect the revised title. 


e A webinar on "Preliminary Insights on UDIN for Bank Audits" was organized on April 7th, 2025, to benefit 
our esteemed members. The session provided valuable insights into the application and significance of the 
UDIN (Unique Document Identification Number) in bank audits. 


e Based on requests received from members, Financial Years 2007—l2 have been added in the dropdown for 
UDIN generation for Form 26A/27BA under the GST Tax Category on the UDIN Portal with effect from 
2\st March 2025. 


e It has been decided to change the data type for capturing figures and values from alphanumeric to numeric 
across all UDIN categories—Certificate, GST & Tax Audit, and Audit & Assurance Functions—in a phased 
manner. The implementation began with the Audit & Assurance Functions category, which went live on 
December 6, 2024, followed by GST & Tax Audit on December 2, 2024, and Certificates on December 28, 
2024. This change aims to ensure uniformity and consistency in the numerical data entered by members 
during UDIN generation. 


(IV) Impact of UDIN 


The Unique Document Identification Number (UDIN) system, introduced by ICAI, has significantly enhanced 
transparency, authenticity, and reliability in professional documentation by preventing forgery and misuse of 
Chartered Accountants’ certifications. Each certified document receives a unique ID, enabling easy verification and 
drastically reducing counterfeit instances. UDIN has streamlined regulatory compliance, allowing authorities to 
efficiently verify documents and reduce fraud, thus fostering a more accountable and ethical professional 
environment. As of June l0, 2025, over |.53 lakh CAs are registered on the UDIN portal, with more than 8.62 
crore UDINs generated across audits, certificates, and tax audits, and over 3.69 crore UDINs verified by regulators, 
banks, and others.

0. BOARD OF STUDIES - ACADEMIC 


The Board of Studies (Academic) plays an instrumental role in shaping the careers of aspiring CA students by 
providing them a comprehensive package of educational resources, guiding them at every stage of their 
academic journey and mentoring them in their goal of becoming a qualified Chartered Accountant. In its 
endeavour to provide a strong foundation of professional knowledge and professional values, the BoS(A) 
provides its students quality Study Materials, Revisionary Test Papers, Mock Test Papers, Suggested Answers 
for each subject of the CA course and also provides Saransh- Last Mile Referencer and Case Scenario 
Booklets. Live Virtual Classes, ICAI Digital Learning Campus and MCQ Paper Practice Assessment 
Dashboard are some of the digital initiatives of BoS(A) to facilitate student learning and preparation for their 
examinations.

Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQ) Paper Practice Assessment Dashboard 


To provide hands-on practice for MCQ-based assessments, the Board of Studies (Academic) has launched the 
MCQ Paper Practice Assessment Dashboard on the BOS Knowledge Portal and ICAI-BOS Mobile App. This 
user-friendly tool helps CA students at all levels—Foundation, Intermediate, and Final—self-assess their 
progress and deepen their understanding of each chapter. It offers a combination of MCQs and case scenario - 
based questions, with options to select difficulty levels (Simple, Medium, Difficult), and allows students to 
attempt 20 MCQs in 20 minutes, with extra time reflected in performance reports. The dashboard also tracks 
paper-wise and chapter-wise performance, with regularly updated content to support continuous preparation.

Success at CA exam 


The Board of Studies (Academic) regularly conducts the “Success at CA Exam” webinar series to guide 
students on strategic exam preparation. Featuring experienced faculty and subject experts, these webinars 
cover study techniques, time management, exam patterns, and tips for tackling challenging topics. They 
also address common student concerns and aim to motivate and prepare students for success. Two webinar 
series are held before each examination across all levels. For the 2024-2025 year, BOS (A) conducted 60 
webinars for three Foundation and Intermediate exams, and 24 webinars for two Final exams. 


Saransh - Last Mile Referencer 


"Saransh" is a comprehensive booklet featuring diagrams, flow charts, and tables summarizing subject topics 
presented in a visually appealing and easy-to-understand format. It serves as a one-stop repository, 
consolidating significant concepts for quick reference and last-minute revision before exams. In the year 
2024-2025, BOS (A) has released twelve subject-wise Saransh booklets for all the subjects of Foundation and 
Intermediate level of CA course curriculum. 


Model Test Paper Booklet 


Model Test Paper is a booklet which act as a valuable question bank, containing multiple Test Papers. The 
papers include a variety of question types, helping students familiarize themselves with different ways 
questions may be framed in the actual exam. The papers provide insight into the structure and format of the 
ICAI exams. In the year 2024-2025, BOS (A) has released in total l8 booklets for various subjects of ICAI 
course curriculum. 


Case Scenario Booklet 


The Case Scenario Booklet is designed to enhance students’ analytical thinking and application-based 
learning. The booklet also helps students better prepare for case-based and integrated questions in the 
examinations. Overall, it fosters a deeper appreciation of the subject matter, promotes interlinking of 
concepts, and helps bridge the gap between academic learning and real-world expectations. In the year 2024- 
2025, BOS (A) has released in total l4 booklets for all subjects of Intermediate and Final level where 30% 
of the assessment is in the form of case scenario based MCQs. 


Launch of ICAI Digital Learning Campus Portal: Self-Paced Online Modules (SPOM) 


The Board of Studies of ICAI launched the ICAI Digital Learning Campus Portal on 7th May 2024, aligning 
with the New Scheme of Education and Training. The portal supports Self-Paced Online Modules (SPOM), 
requiring 40 learning hours each for SET A (Corporate & Economic Laws) and SET B (Strategic Cost & 
Performance Management), and 20 hours each for SET C and SET D, can choose one paper from |0 Papers of 
SET C and one paper from 4 papers of SET D, available on the ICAI Digital Learning Campus Portal at 
https://Ims.icai.org/login The Self-Paced Online Modules (SPOM) are exclusively accessible to Final Course 
students, offering them the flexibility to learn at their own pace, anytime and anywhere. These modules are 
available at no additional cost. Students can monitor their learning progress through a ICAI Digital Learning

Study Materials for Select Subjects under MRA/MOUs with various Foreign Accounting Bodies 


ICAI is endeavoring to provide mobility to its members by having the ICAI qualification recognized in 
different parts of the world. Accounting bodies worldwide mutually recognize the qualification of ICAI for 
the benefit of members at either ends. Through these agreements, members of one institute can gain 
membership in the other by passing a limited number of bridging examination papers and fulfilling specific 
criteria (e.g., good standing, no disciplinary issues, original qualification through examination). For those

(IRELAND), ICAEW, ICAN, SAICA, AUSTRALIA AND NEW ZEALAND. 


Study Materials for Select Subjects under Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Scheme 


Regulation 53C. Enrolment of Overseas Citizen of India Professional Accountants was inserted in the Chartered 
Accountants Regulations, 988 vide Notification No.l-CA(7)/54/204 dated 22"4 July 204. As per Regulation 
53C(l), an Overseas Citizen of India holding professional accountancy qualification shall be recognised as a 
member of the Institute on completion of such examination, training and other modules as listed out in Schedule 
‘B’ to the regulations. Schedule B contains the Scheme for enrolment of Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) 
Professional Accountants. As per this Scheme, to be eligible for membership of the Institute, an OCI having 
chartered accountant or certified public accountant qualification is required to pass the First Level Test and the Second 
Level Test and comply with the other provisions of the Scheme. Accordingly, BOS (A) has webhosted the study 
materials of following subjects:

0.2 BOARD OF STUDIES-OPERATION 


Board of Studies - Operations is a key non-standing committee of the Institute, focused on providing 
world-class training to Chartered Accountancy (CA) students. It conducts mandatory training programs 
such as Orientation, Information Technology (IT), Advanced IT, and Management & Communication Skills 
through IT and Soft Skills Centres across India. The Board also organizes Four-Week Residential Programs 
at Centres of Excellence in Hyderabad and Jaipur, along with various student-focused events including 
International, National, State, and Branch-level Conferences, seminars, workshops, sports competitions, 
festivals, industrial visits, counselling sessions, and national talent contests. Scholarships are provided to 
eligible CA students under various categories. The Board aims to equip students with essential professional 
and interpersonal skills—such as management, communication, presentation, and oratory skills—to meet 
evolving industry demands and enhance the overall image of the CA profession.

ii. XBRL 


For the effective participation of the regulators, technologists, corporates and academicians in the endeavor of the 
Institute for the promotion of XBRL in India, the Institute has facilitated the incorporation of XBRL India as a 
section 25 company (currently under Section 8 of Companies Act, 203) with the main objective of promoting and 
encouraging the adoption of XBRL in India as the standard for electronic business reporting in India through 
development of taxonomies, facilitation of education and training on XBRL. Also, XBRL India has taken 
membership of XBRL International to facilitate and get updates of XBRL filing globally. XBRL India is an 
established Indian jurisdiction of XBRL International. 


Currently, XBRL India is developing and maintaining XBRL taxonomies for Ministry of Corporate Affairs 
(MCA).

.2 ICAI- Accounting Research Foundation (ARF) 


ICAI Accounting Research Foundation (ICAI ARF) was established in January, 999 to be developed as an 
academy for imparting, spreading and promoting knowledge, learning, education and understanding in the various 
fields related to the profession of accountancy. The following is the detail of projects undertaken by ICAI ARF: 


० Indian Railways: 


Indian Railways, the fourth largest railway network in the world after the United States, Russia and China, is 
undertaking several initiatives towards Accounting Reforms in line with generally accepted accounting principles. 
In its journey of accounting reforms, the Indian Railways had initiated exercise of preparation of its Accrual Based 
Financial Statements in 204, marking a major shift towards enhanced financial transparency and accountability. 
Since the inception of this initiative, the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) and its Accounting 
Research Foundation (ICAI ARF) have played a pivotal role in supporting these reforms. ICAI ARF has been 
instrumental in guiding Indian Railways through the migration to an accrual-based accounting system. ICAI ARF 
have successfully prepared the Accrual Based Financial Statements for all Zonal Railways and Production Units 
from the financial year 205-6 to 2022-23. 


Work Completed in last one year 


e Accrual Based Financial Statements (ABFS) of Indian Railways for the year 202l-22 and 2022-23 
submitted. Several initiatives towards environment Sustainability undertaken by the Indian Railways have 
been reflected in the financial statements for 2022-23. It will be a milestone in the history of Government of 
India that accrual based to financial statements has been prepared. 


e Pilot Study to develop framework for Clearance of CWIP and transfer to FAR to be undertaken over NR 
based on the CWIP data. 


Work in progress: 


ABEFS of Indian Railways for the year 2023-24. 


e Treasuries and Accounts Department, Government of Tamil Nadu: ICAI ARF has undertaken the task of 
rewriting of regulatory framework governing Treasury and Accounts in the State, primarily (i) Treasury Code, 
(ii) Accounts Code (iii) Pay and Accounts Office Manual and review of all forms used by the State and 


[भाग ता--खण्ड 4] भारत का राजपत्र : असाधारण 309 


recommendations on redundancies, improvements, simplification and new forms to be documented as part of 
the official code documents of the State. The ICAI has completed the project during the year and submitted the 
same to Commissioner of Treasuries and Accounts on June 9, 2024. 


e Indian Ports Association (IPA): ICAI ARF has been assigned the task to prepare common accounting 
framework for |] major ports for compliance with Major Ports Authorities Act, 202] and MPA (Accounts & 
Audit) Rules, 202l. The Common Framework for the preparation of annual accounts for Major Ports and 
Significant Accounting Policies document for all ports submitted to IPA. Both the documents have been 
forwarded by the IPA to Ministry of Shipping Port and Waterways (MoPSW) for notifying in consultation with 
CAG for implementation in all Major Ports and also to notify the timelines for the placement of audited annual 
accounts of Major Ports. The matter is under consideration of Ministry of Shipping Port and Waterways. 


e Certificate Course for Accountants of Panchayats & Municipal Bodies: ICAI ARF executed the project of 
Certificate Courses for Accountants of Panchayats and Municipal Bodies through Board for Local Bodies 
Accountants Certification (i.c., BLoAC established under ICAI ARF). The Committee on Public and 
Government Financial Management (CPGFM) of ICAI is actively involved in development of course material 
and coordination for the conduct of the courses. The courses were formally launched on 6" November 2023 
(Audit Diwas) and the registrations of these courses were initiated on [7 December 2023 through a dedicated 
website https://lba.icaiarf.org.in/ Approx. 3699 candidates have registered for this course during the year. As 
per structure of course, two offline exams (screening and main exam) are being held. Under screening exam, 
basic of accounting is covered and under main exam, panchayat/ municipal bodies specific accounting is 
covered. ICAI exam system has been replicated for the certificate courses exam after little modification 
(considering less registrations received) but robustness of ICAI exam system is maintained.

.5 The Institute of Social Auditors of India (ISAT) 


The Institute of Social Auditors of India (ISAD) is incorporated under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 20l3 on 
October 07, 2022 under the aegis of The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) as Self-Regulatory 
Organization with prime objective to be a leading institution for developing an independent, ethical and world-class 
Social Impact Assessors (earlier Social Auditors) responding to needs and expectations of the stakeholders. ISAI 
enrol, regulate, and develop Social Impact Assessors (earlier Social Auditors) in an independent and transparent 
manner and also work on capacity building of the Social Impact Assessors through continuous professional 
education and training. 


(0) Concept of Social Impact Assessors (earlier Social Auditors) 


The Finance Minister in the Budget speech of 20!9-2020 for the first time proposed the concept of a Social Stock 
Exchange which will be “under the regulatory ambit of Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBIJ) for listing 
social enterprises and voluntary organizations working for the realization of a social welfare objective so that they 
can raise capital as equity, debt or as units like a mutual fund.” Subsequently, the Securities and Exchange Board of 
India (SEBI) vide its notification dated 25th July 2022 has amended the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 20l8 (“ICDR Regulations”), SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 20l5 (“LODR Regulations”) and SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 20l2 (“AIF 
Regulations”) to provide a broad framework for Social Stock Exchange. SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure 
Requirements) (Third Amendment) Regulations, 2022 defines Social Auditors as an individual registered with a 
Self Regulatory Organization under the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India or such other agency, as may be 
specified by the Board, who has qualified a certification program conducted by National Institute of Securities 
Market and holds a valid certificate. SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirement) (Third Amendment) 
Regulation, 2023 dated December 2l, 2023 substituted the word “Auditor” appearing in the words and expression 
“Social Auditor” with the words “Impact Assessor”. 


(ID) Governing Board of ISAT 
ISAI functions through its Governing Board which comprises of minimum of Twelve Directors i.e. 


e Chairperson, having rich experience in social sector/ impact assessment or he may be from a renowned 
academic institution. 


e Five Central Council members of ICAI/ Sustainability Reporting Standards Board with relevant experience. 
e One person to be nominated by Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI). 


e One person to be nominated by Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA)/ Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA)/ 
Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment. 


e One person nominated by Capacity Building Fund. 
e One person nominated by Social Stock Exchange. 
e One member from thematic areas of the social sector. 


e One member having cross sectoral experience in social sectors.

2. Quality Review Board (QRB) 


The Quality Review Board (QRB) has been constituted by the Central Government of India u/s 28A of the 
Chartered Accountants Act, |949 as an independent oversight body engaged in monitoring the quality of services 
provided by the Chartered Accountants in India. The constitution of the QRB includes a chairperson, 5 members 
appointed by the Central Government and 5 members nominated from the Council of ICAI. Although, the 
provisions of Sec. 28B of the Act authorizes the QRB to review all kinds of services provided by the members of 
the ICAI, however, the Board currently is involved in review of audit services, only. As per Section 28B of the 
Chartered Accountants Act, 949, the Quality Review Board shall perform the following functions: - 


e To make recommendations to the Council with regard to the quality of services provided by the members of 
the Institute. 


e To review the quality of services provided by the members of the Institute including audit services. 


e To guide the members of the Institute to improve the quality of services and adherence to the various 
statutory and other regulatory requirements. 


e To forward cases of non-compliance with various statutory and regulatory requirements by the members of 
the Institute or firms, noticed by it during the course of its reviews, to the Disciplinary Directorate for its 
examination. 


After the formation of National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) by the Central Government in the year 
208, the QRB has been involved in review of the quality of the audit services w.r.t entities not falling under Rule 3 
of NFRA Rules, 208. In order to make the process of quality reviews more comprehensive the Board has taken 
following key steps during the year 2024-25: 


e Modification in the criteria of selection of companies / audit firms in order to make the selection process 
more robust and inclusive. Modified selection criteria can be referred at “Procedure for Quality Review of 
Audit Services of Audit Firms (Revised)” hosted at website of the Board www.grbca.in 


e Modification in the “Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for conducting Quality Reviews”, thus reducing 
the overall time taken in completion of audit quality reviews. The revised SOP is hosted at the website of the 
Board. 


During the period covered by the Report, 52 reviews of audit quality have been conducted by the Quality Review 
Board and Quality Review Group I & II and out of these 52 reviews:

INDEPENDENT AUDITOR'S REPORT 
To The Council, 
The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India 
Report on the Audit of the Financial Statements 
Opinion 


We have audited the accompanying financial statements of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (“the 
Institute”), which comprise the Balance Sheet as at 3! March 2025, the Income and Expenditure Account, the 
Statement of Cash Flows for the year then ended, and notes to the financial statements, including a summary of 
the significant accounting policies and other explanatory information (herein after referred to as “financial 
statements”) in which are incorporated the returns/financial statements audited by the branch auditors of the 
Institute’s Decentralized offices, Overseas offices, Centres of Excellence, Regional Councils and their Branches. 


In our opinion and to the best of our information and according to the explanations given to us, the aforesaid 
financial statements give the information required by the Chartered Accountants Act, !949 (as amended upto 
date) in the manner so required and give a true and fair view in conformity with the accounting principles 
generally accepted in India of the state of affairs of the Institute as at 3! March 2025, its surplus and its cash 
flows for the year ended on that date. 


Basis for Opinion 


We conducted our audit in accordance with the Standards on Auditing (SAs) issued by the Institute of Chartered 
Accountants of India. Our responsibilities under those standards are further described in the ‘Auditor’s 
Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements’ section of our report. We are independent of the 
Institute in accordance with the ethical requirements that are relevant to our audit of the financial statements and 
we have fulfilled our ethical responsibilities in accordance with these requirements and the Code of Ethics. We 
believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion. 


Responsibilities of Management and those Charged with Governance for the Financial Statements 


The Institute's Management and those Charged with Governance is responsible for the preparation of these 
financial statements that give a true and fair view of the financial position, financial performance and cash flows 
of the Institute in accordance with the Chartered Accountants Act, 949 (“the Act”). This responsibility also 
includes maintenance of adequate accounting records in accordance with the provisions of the Act for 
safeguarding the assets of the Institute and for preventing and detecting frauds and other irregularities; selection 
and application of appropriate accounting policies; making judgements and estimates that are reasonable and 
prudent; and design, implementation and maintenance of adequate internal financial controls, that were operating 
effectively for ensuring the accuracy and completeness of the accounting records, relevant to the preparation and 
presentation of the financial statements that give a true and fair view and are free from material misstatement, 
whether due to fraud or error. 


In preparing the financial statements, the management is responsible for assessing the Institute’s ability to 
continue as a going concern, disclosing, as applicable, matters related to going concern and using the going 
concern basis of accounting unless management either intends to liquidate the Institute or to cease operations, or 
has no realistic alternative but to do so. 


Those charged with governance are also responsible for overseeing the Institute’s financial reporting process. 


Auditor’s Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements 


Our objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements as a whole are free from 
material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and to issue an auditor’s report that includes our opinion. 


[भाग ता--खण्ड 4] भारत का राजपत्र : असाधारण 323 


Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance, but is not a guarantee that an audit conducted in accordance 
with SAs will always detect a material misstatement when it exists. Misstatements can arise from fraud or error 
and are considered material if, individually or in the aggregate, they could reasonably be expected to influence 
the economic decisions of users taken on the basis of these financial statements. 


As part of an audit in accordance with SAs, we exercise professional judgment and maintain professional 
skepticism throughout the audit. We also: 


7 Identify and assess the risks of material misstatement of the financial statements, whether due to fraud or 
error, design and perform audit procedures responsive to those risks, and obtain audit evidence that is 
sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion. The risk of not detecting a material 
misstatement resulting from fraud is higher than for one resulting from error, as fraud may involve 
collusion, forgery, intentional omissions, misrepresentations, or the override of internal controls. 


: Obtain an understanding of internal controls relevant to the audit in order to design audit procedures that 
are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the 
effectiveness of the Institute’s internal controls. 


: Evaluate the appropriateness of accounting policies used and the reasonableness of accounting estimates 
and related disclosures made by management. 


: Conclude on the appropriateness of the management’s use of the going concern basis of accounting and, 
based on the audit evidence obtained, whether a material uncertainty exists related to events or 
conditions that may cast significant doubt on the Institute’s ability to continue as a going concern. If we 
conclude that a material uncertainty exists, we are required to draw attention in our auditor’s report to 
the related disclosures in the financial statements or, if such disclosures are inadequate, to modify our 
opinion. Our conclusions are based on the audit evidence obtained up to the date of our auditor’s report. 
However, future events or conditions may cause the Institute to cease to continue as a going concern. 


| Evaluate the overall presentation, structure and content of the financial statements, including the 
disclosures, and whether the financial statements represent the underlying transactions and events in a 
manner that achieve fair presentation. 


Materiality is the magnitude of misstatements in the financial statements that, individually or in aggregate, makes 
it probable that the economic decisions of a reasonably knowledgeable user of the financial statements may be 
influenced. We consider quantitative materiality and qualitative factors in (i) planning the scope of our audit 
work and in evaluating the results of our work; and (ii) to evaluate the effect of any identified misstatements in 
the financial statements. 


We communicate with those charged with governance regarding, among other matters, the planned scope and 
timing of the audit and significant audit findings, including any significant deficiencies in internal controls that 
we identify during our audit. 


We also provide those charged with governance with a statement that we have complied with relevant ethical 
requirements regarding independence, and to communicate with them all relationships and other matters that may 
reasonably be thought to bear on our independence, and where applicable, related safeguards. 


Other Matters 


a) There are number of study circles, study chapters authorized by the Institute to facilitate continuous 
professional education activities for members in India and abroad. The Institute has represented that these 
study circles/chapters are separate entities and accordingly their financials statements are not required to 
be consolidated. We have relied on this representation. 


b) We did not audit the financial statements/information of the Institute’s Decentralized Offices, Overseas 
Offices, Centers of Excellence, Regional Councils and their branches (collectively known as Branches) 
whose financial statements reflect total assets of Rs ,33,459 Lakhs as at 3l March 2025, total revenue of 
Rs |8,299 Lakhs for the year ended 3 March 2025 and cash & cash equivalent of Rs 5,22] Lakhs as at 3 ] 


324 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY [PART III—SEC.4] 


March 2025 as considered in the financial statements. The financial statements/information of these 
Branches have been audited by the Branch Auditors whose reports have been furnished to us by the 
management and our opinion in so far as it relates to the amounts and disclosures included in respect of 
such Branches, is based solely on the reports of Branch Auditors. 


Cc 


~— 


We did not audit the financial statements/information of the Institute’s Singapore Branch and Yamuna 
Nagar Branch of Northern India Regional Council of the Institute which reflects total assets of Rs 47 
Lakhs as at 3l March 2025, total revenue of Rs 5l Lakhs for the year ended 3] March 2025 and cash & 
cash equivalent of Rs 28 Lakhs as at 3l March 2025 as considered in the financial statements. Such 
financial statements/information are unaudited and have been furnished to us by the management and our 
report on the financial statement, in so far as it relates to the amount and disclosure is based solely on the 
unaudited financial statement/ information. According to the information and explanation given to us, this 
financial statements/ information is not material to the Institute. 


Our opinion is not modified in respect of above matters. 
Report on Other Regulatory Requirements 
Further, we report that: 


a) We have sought and obtained all the information and explanations which to the best of our knowledge and 
belief were necessary for the purpose of our audit; 


b) In our opinion, proper books of account have been kept by the Institute so far as appears from our 
examination of those books and proper returns adequate for the purpose of our audit have been received 
from the branches not visited by us. 


c) The reports on the accounts of the branches of the Institute audited by branch auditors have been sent to us 
and have been properly dealt with by us in preparing this report. 


d) The Balance Sheet, the Statement of Income and Expenditure, and the Statement of Cash Flow dealt with 
by this Report are in agreement with the books of accounts and with the returns received from the 
branches not visited by us.

Notes forming part of the Financial Statements for the year 2024-25 
I. General Information 


The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India ("the Institute or ICAI"), having its Head Office at 
New Delhi, was established on Ist July 949 by an Act of Parliament viz. The Chartered Accountants 
Act, 949 for the purpose of regulation and development of the profession of Chartered Accountants 
in India. In terms of the said Act, the Council of the Institute is entrusted with the task of managing 
the affairs of the Institute. For this purpose, the Council has constituted 5 Regional Councils, one each 
at Mumbai, Kolkata, Kanpur, Chennai and New Delhi, 5 Decentralised Offices, 2 Centres of 
Excellence, [77 branches and 2 overseas offices in Dubai & Singapore. 


2. Significant Accounting Policies 
2.0i Basis of Preparation 


The financial statements comprising Balance Sheet, Statement of Income and Expenditure Account, 
Statement of Cash Flow and Notes thereon are prepared in accordance with the Generally Accepted 
Accounting Principles in India (Indian GAAP) and The Chartered Accountants Act,l949. Indian 
GAAP here comprises of the accounting standards and other pronouncements issued by the Institute 
of Chartered Accountants of India. The financial statements are prepared on historical cost 
convention, going concern and on accrual basis unless other wise stated. The accounting polices 
adopted in the preparation of the financial statements are consistent with those followed in the 
previous year, unless stated otherwise. 


2.02 Use of Estimates 


The preparation of the financial statements in conformity with Indian GAAP requires the Management 
to make estimates and assumptions considered in the reported amounts of assets and liabilities 
(including contingent liabilities) and the reported income and expenses of the year. The Management 
believes that the estimates used in preparation of the financial statements are prudent and reasonable. 
Actual results could differ from the estimates and the differences between the actual results and the 
estimates are recognised in the periods in which the results are known / materialised. 


2.03 Inventories 


Inventories comprise publications, study materials, stationery and other stores. Inventories are valued 
at the lower of cost based on first in first out method ("FIFO") and the net realisable value after 
providing for obsolescence and other losses, where considered necessary. 


Cost includes all charges in bringing the goods to the point of sale, including other levies, transit 
insurance and incidental charges.

Cash and cash equivalents 


Cash comprises cash on hand. Cash equivalents are short-term balances (with an original maturity of 
three months or less from the date of acquisition), highly liquid investments that are readily 
convertible into known amounts of cash and which are subject to insignificant risk of changes in 
value. Fixed Deposits with original maturity of less than three months are considered as cash and cash 
equivalents. Deposits with original maturity for more than 3 months but less than 2 months are 
considered as bank deposits under "Other bank balances". 


Statement of Cash Flow 


Cash flows are reported using the indirect method, whereby net surplus is adjusted for the effects of 
transactions of non-cash nature and any deferrals or accruals of past or future cash receipts or 
payments. The cash flows from operating, investing and financing activities of the Institute are 
segregated based on the available information.

Property, Plant and Equipment 


Property, Plant and Equipment is recognised when it is probable that future economic benefits 
associated with the item will flow to the Institute and the cost of the item can be measured reliably. 
Property, Plant and Equipment are carried at cost less accumulated depreciation and accumulated 
impairment losses, if any. The cost of Property, Plant and Equipment comprises its purchase price net 
of any trade discounts and rebates, import duties and other taxes (other than those subsequently 
recoverable from the tax authorities), directly attributable expenditure on making the asset ready for 
its intended use. Other incidental expenses and interest on borrowings attributable to acquisition of 


330 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY [PART III—SEC.4] 


qualifying Property, Plant and Equipment up to the date the asset is ready for its intended use are also 
capitalised. 


2.08 Intangible Assets 


Intangible assets are carried at cost less accumulated amortisation and accumulated impairment losses, 
if any. The cost of intangible assets comprises its purchase price net of any trade discounts and 
rebates, import duties and other taxes (other than those subsequently recoverable from the tax 
authorities), directly attributable expenditure on making the asset ready for its intended use, other 
incidental expenses and interest on borrowings attributable to acquisition of qualifying assets up to the 
date the asset is ready for its intended use. Subsequent expenditure on intangible assets after its 
purchase / completion is capitalised only if such expenditure results in an increase in the future 
benefits from such asset beyond its previously assessed standard of performance. 


2.09 Capital Work in Progress 


Expenditure incurred on construction/ development of assets which is not ready for their intended use 
is carried at cost less impairment, if any, under Capital Work-in-Progress. The cost includes the 
purchase cost including import duties, non-refundable taxes, if any, and directly attributable costs. 


2.40 Depreciation and amortization 
A) Depreciable amount for assets is the cost of an asset, or other amount substituted as cost. 


Depreciation on Property, Plant and Equipment is provided monthly prorata on the written down 
value method at the following rates as approved by the Council.

B) Carrying amount of building on Leasehold land is amortised over the lease term . 
C) Intangible assets are amortised on straight line method over three years. 
2. Revenue recognition 
The Revenue is recognised as follows: 


i) Distance education fee received from the students is recognised by proportionate completion method 
over the duration of the respective courses. 


ii) Class room training fee comprises fee received for Management Communication Skills Course 
("MCS"), Integrated Course on Information Technology & Soft Skills ("ICITSS"), Advanced 
Integrated Course on Information Technology & Soft Skills ("AICITSS") and Orientation 
Programme ("OP").The income for classroom training and revisionary classes is recognised when 
services are rendered and related costs are incurred. 


iii) Examination fee is recognised as revenue when the Institute renders the related service i.e. when 
the examinations are conducted. 


iv) Seminar fee is recognised as revenue when the Institute renders the related service i.e. when the 
seminars are conducted. 


v) Membership fee comprising of annual membership fee (including fee for certificate of practice and 
restoration fee) and entrance fee is recognised as under: 


a) Annual membership fee (including fee for certificate of practice) is recognised as income when 
it becomes due for the year. Restoration of membership fee is recognised when it is received.

Investment 


a) 


The Institute’s investments comprise of instruments in the form of domestic government securities 
issued by Central and State Governments, fixed deposits with scheduled banks domiciled in India 
and shares in Not-for-Profit entities. 


Investments are classified as current and long term investments in accordance with AS 3 
Investments. Current investments are those that are readily realisable and intended to be held for 
not more than one year from the date on which such investments are made. A long term investment 
is an investment other than a current investment. 


Investments are initially recorded at cost and the cost includes acquisition costs such as brokerage, 
fees and duties. Accrued interest paid at the time of purchase is setoff against receipt of interest. 


Investments in the form of domestic government securities issued by Central and State 
Governments are available for use freely at the discretion of the Council except to the extent of 
total of the earmarked funds. 


At each balance sheet date, current investments are carried at lower of cost and fair value. The fair 
value is determined on an individual basis. The long term investments are usually carried at cost. 
However,when there is a decline, other than temporary, in the value of a long term investment, the 
carrying amount is reduced to recognise the decline. The premium paid at the time of purchase is 
amortised over the remaining maturity of the investments. Amortisation of premium is adjusted 
against the income under head ‘Interest from Investments. 


Foreign Currency Transaction 


Transactions in foreign currencies are accounted at the exchange rates prevailing on the date of the 
transaction. 


Foreign currency monetary items outstanding at the balance sheet date are restated at the year- end 
rates. Non-monetary items are carried at historical cost. 


332 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY [PART III—SECc.4] 


Exchange differences arising on settlement / restatement of foreign currency monetary assets and liabilities 
are recognised as income or expense in the Statement of Income and Expenditure. 


2.5 Employee benefits 


Employee benefits include provident fund, gratuity fund, compensated absence, long service awards, 
pension scheme and post-employment medical benefits. 


i) Short term employee benefits 


The undiscounted amount of short-term employee benefits (i.e. salary, allowances, exgratia etc) 
expected to be paid in exchange for the services rendered by employees are recognised during the year 
when the employees render the service. The short-term employee benefits are expected to occur 
within twelve months after the end of the period in which the eligible employee renders the related 
service. 


The cost of short-term compensated absences is accounted as under : 


a) Incase of accumulated compensated absences, when employees render the service that increase 
their entitlement of future compensated absences; and 


b) Incase of non-accumulating compensated absences, when the absences occur. 
ii) Post-employment benefits 


Post-employment benefits are the benefits to eligible employees, other than termination benefits, 
which are payable after the completion of employment. Accounting of post- employment benefits 
depends upon the classification of relevant plans as either defined benefit plan (DBP) or defined 
contribution plan (DCP). The post-employment benefit plans where the Institute pays fixed 
contributions into a separate entity or fund and it will have no obligation to pay further contributions if 
the separate entity or fund does not hold sufficient assets to all employee benefits relating to employee 
service in the current and prior period. On the other hand, post-employment benefit plans other than 
those classified as DCP are classified as DBP. 


A.2 Defined Benefits Plans 
a) Gratuity 


For defined benefit plans in the form of gratuity, the cost of providing benefits is determined using 
the Projected Unit Credit Method, with actuarial valuations being carried out at each balance sheet 
date. Actuarial gains and losses are recognised in the Statement of Income and Expenditure in the 
period in which they occur. Past service cost is recognised immediately to the extent that the 
benefits are already vested and otherwise is amortised on a straight-line basis over the average 
period until the benefits become vested. The retirement benefit obligation recognised represent the 
present value of the defined benefit obligation as adjusted for unrecognised past service cost, as 
reduced by the fair value of scheme assets. Any asset resulting from this calculation is limited to 
past service cost, plus the present value of available refunds and reductions in future contributions 
to the schemes. Gratuity liability is funded with Life Insurance Corporation of India. 


b) Provident Fund 


The contribution towards provident fund scheme to The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India 
Provident Fund Trust (‘the Trust’) is considered as defined benefit plan and charged as an expense 
based on the amount of contribution required to be made and when services are rendered by the 
eligible employees. The Trust is managed by the governing body elected by the Institute and 
settles claim of the employees as and when they arise. Any shortfall arising out of actuarial 
liability of the PF Trust and any shortfall in return on investment during the year as per the 
valuation report is claimed by the trust and is paid by the Institute. 


The present value of the defined benefit obligations are ascertained by an independent actuary as per 
the requirements of Accounting Standard (AS) - 5 Employee Benefits. 


c) Pension scheme 


The Institute offers its eligible employees benefits in the form of pension. The present value of the 
obligation as at the balance sheet date is recognised based on the actuarial valuation. Pension 
liability is funded with Life Insurance Corporation of India.

e) Other Long-term employee benefits- Compensated Absences 


Compensated absences which are not expected to occur within twelve months after the end of the 
period in which the employee renders the related service are recognised as a liability at the present 
value of the defined benefit obligation as at the balance sheet date based on the actuarial valuation. 


Leases 


The Institute classifies the leases as Finance and Operating Lease for accounting and disclosure 
purposes. The leases where the Institute assumes substantially all the risks and rewards of the 
ownership are classified as finance leases. The leases where the lessor and not the Institute assumes 
substantially all the risks and rewards of the ownership are classified as operating leases. 


Lease rental under operating leases are recognised in the statement of income and expenditure on 
straight-line basis over the lease term. In case of Finance Lease, assets are capitalised at lower of fair 
value of the leased asset and present value of minimum lease payments. The lease payments are 
apportioned between the finance charge and repayment of lease liability. Leased assets are depreciated 
over the shorter of lease term or useful life of the asset. 


Impairment of Property, Plant and Equipment and intangible assets 


The carrying value of assets at each balance sheet date are reviewed for impairment. If any indication 
of impairment exists, the recoverable amount of such assets is estimated and impairment recognised, if 
the carrying amount of these assets exceeds their recoverable amount. The recoverable amount is the 
greater of the net selling price and their value in use. Value in use is arrived at by discounting the 
future cash flows to their present value based on an appropriate discount factor. When there is 
indication that an impairment loss recognised for an asset in earlier accounting periods no longer 
exists or may have decreased, such reversal of impairment loss is recognised in the statement of 
income and expenditure. 


Taxes on income 


The Institute is registered under section 0(23C)(iv) of the Income Tax Act, 96l. As such, no 
provision for current income tax and deferred tax is considered necessary. 


Provisions and Contingencies 


A provision is recognised when there is a present obligation as a result of past events and it is probable 
that an outflow of resources will be required to settle the obligation in respect of which a reliable 
estimate can be made. 


Contingent liability is a possible obligation that arises from past events and the existence of which will 
be confirmed only by the occurrence or non-occurrence of one or more uncertain future events not 
wholly within the control of the Institute, or is a present obligation that arises from past event but is 
not recognised because either it is not probable that an outflow of resources embodying economic 
benefits will be required to settle the obligation, or a reliable estimate of the amount of the obligation 
cannot be made. Contingent liabilities are disclosed and not recognised. 


Contingent assets are neither recognised nor disclosed.

29.0l Contingent liabilities and commitments 


a. Contingent liabilities 2024-25 2023-24 


i) Claims against the Institute not acknowledged as debts 2,480 ,844 


ii) In financial year 208-9,the Institute received two show cause notices of = 5,797 lakhs from the 
Additional Director General, Goods and Service Tax Intelligence for payment of service tax on 
annual fee, certificate of practice fee, entrance fee, Seminar Fees and Coaching Class Fees etc. The 
Institute is of the opinion that it is not liable to service tax and filed writ petition No. 3957/20I9 in 
High Court of Delhi in April 209. Additional Director General, DGCEI, Kochi filed a Counter 
affidavit against the aforesaid writ petition in October 20l9 against which the Institute filed a 
rejoinder affidavit in December 209. The matter is being adjourned from time to time. 


b. Capital Commitments 
2024-25 2023-24

29.02 Other Receivables in Note 7 # include = 97 Lakhs for stamp duty refund receivable on cancellation of 
principal and supplementary agreements of acquiring property at Nagpur. 


Vide judgement dated 03.07.2023, the Chief Controlling Revenue Authority, Pune in Appeal No. 38 & 
39/204 had ordered refund of stamp duty of = [52.66 lakhs and % 46.75 lakhs respectively paid by ICAI 
on the supplementary sale agreement dated 03.08.202 registered on 7.09.20l2. However, the claim of = 
44.34 lakhs was declined due to non-entitlement against assignment of lease hold rights in land. Provision 
has been made for हैं 44.34 lakhs this year and हें 5.27 lakhs also for the 0% amount of = 52.66 lakhs as 
the same will be deducted as per Section 22A of the Maharashtra Stamp Rules 939. The net amount of < 
37.39 lakhs is realizable. 


Writ petitions bearing Nos. 2987 of 2024 (challenging Appeal No. 39 of 204) and Writ Petition No. 2988 
of 2024 (challenging Appeal No. 38 of 204) filed before the Bombay High Court are pending. 


29.03 The report of the detailed review of various reserves and earmarked funds received last year is under 
review to restructure these funds as per the present requirements and functioning of the Institute. 


29.04 The quoted investments in Government securities have been made for the long term. The market price of 


346 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY [PART III—SEC.4] 


these bonds fluctuate on a day to day basis, since the intention of the Institute is to hold these securities for 
long term, any temporary decline in the value of these securities against the cost is not provided for as the 
management is confident that in the long run the market price of these securities will be more than its cost. 


29.05 The inter unit transactions of units with Head Office pertaining to Income and Expenditure of current 
accounts stand reconciled. The net impact of difference of amount payable and receivable between Head 
Office and units of = l05 lakhs has been shown under Income & Expenditure Account as prior period 
income which has been approved by the Management. In case of balances between the units of ICAI 
(other than Head Office) related to receivables and payables, the unreconciled net difference of = 47 
lakhs has been classified under “ Other Receivables". 


29.06 The study circles, study chapters and overseas chapters are separate entities and their accounts are not 
consolidated. 


29.07 Steps are being taken to renew the lease period of land expired in some of units. Renewal Lease Premium 
shall become due once confirmation is received from the relevant authorities. 


29.08 The Institute is registered under section 0(23C)(iv) of the Income Tax Act, 96l. As such, no provision 
for current income tax and deferred tax is considered necessary. 


29.09 As part of the process regarding compliance with Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises Development Act 
2006, the Institute has received information from certain vendors at Head Office stating their status as 
vendors registered with notified authority. 


With regard to the vendors at branches and other locations, steps have already been initiated for the 
identification of vendors and the same will be complied with once the process is complete.

32. Segment Reporting 


The Institute's operations are confined to "regulation and development of the profession of Chartered Accountancy" 
and predominantly spread in India. Hence all its operations fall under single segment within the meaning of 
Accounting Standard (AS) - !7 Segment Reporting.
